PRELIMINARY AND FINAL DECLARATIONS OF DISCLOSURE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Preliminary and Final Declarations of Disclosure — Information Sheet concerns the marriage of Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, who were married on June 14, 2015, in connection with a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, legal separation, or nullity contemplated in the California superior court for Sacramento County. It describes California's statutory financial-disclosure framework under Family Code sections 2100 through 2113 — the Legislature's stated purpose for requiring disclosure, what a preliminary declaration of disclosure and a final declaration of disclosure must each contain and when each must be served, the limited circumstances in which the parties may mutually waive the final declaration, and the consequences the statute states for noncompliance. It is not itself a preliminary or final declaration of disclosure, does not itself satisfy either party's disclosure obligations, and does not determine what disclosure is legally required in any specific case; only the actual Judicial Council forms, completed, executed under penalty of perjury, and served, can do that.

THE LEGISLATURE'S STATED PURPOSE: FULL DISCLOSURE AND A CONTINUING DUTY TO UPDATE
California's Family Code sets out the Legislature's own findings and declared purpose for the mandatory financial-disclosure framework that applies in dissolution, legal-separation, and nullity proceedings. The Legislature states that it is the policy of the State of California to marshal, preserve, and protect community and quasi-community assets and liabilities that exist at the date of separation so as to avoid dissipation of the community estate before distribution; to ensure fair and sufficient child and spousal support awards; and to achieve a proper division of community and quasi-community assets and liabilities on dissolution or nullity of marriage or legal separation of the parties. The Legislature further states that sound public policy favors reducing the adversarial nature of marital dissolution and its attendant costs by fostering full disclosure and cooperative discovery, and that, to promote this policy, a full and accurate disclosure of all assets and liabilities in which one or both parties have or may have an interest — together with a disclosure of all income and expenses — must be made in the early stages of a dissolution or legal-separation proceeding, regardless of whether an asset or liability is characterized as community or separate. The statute expressly states that each party has a continuing duty to immediately, fully, and accurately update and augment that disclosure to the extent there have been any material changes, so that by the time the parties reach an agreement resolving these issues, or by the time of trial on these issues, each party has full and complete knowledge of the relevant underlying facts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) It is the policy of the State of California (1) to marshal, preserve, and protect community and quasi-community assets and liabilities that exist at the date of separation so as to avoid dissipation of the community estate before distribution, (2) to ensure fair and sufficient child and spousal support awards, and (3) to achieve a division of community and quasi-community assets and liabilities on the dissolution or nullity of marriage or legal separation of the parties as provided under California law. (b) Sound public policy further favors the reduction of the adversarial nature of marital dissolution and the attendant costs by fostering full disclosure and cooperative discovery. (c) In order to promote this public policy, a full and accurate disclosure of all assets and liabilities in which one or both parties have or may have an interest must be made in the early stages of a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties, regardless of the characterization as community or separate, together with a disclosure of all income and expenses of the parties. Moreover, each party has a continuing duty to immediately, fully, and accurately update and augment that disclosure to the extent there have been any material changes so that at the time the parties enter into an agreement for the resolution of any of these issues, or at the time of trial on these issues, each party will have a full and complete knowledge of the relevant underlying facts."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2100(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), the Legislature's findings and stated purpose for requiring disclosure, and each party's continuing duty to update (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2100.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's stated legislative purpose for its financial-disclosure framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage, dissolution, or legal separation, and not a claim about what disclosure is legally required in any specific case. This clause quotes subdivisions (a) through (c) of a single statutory section (Family Code section 2100); no additional independent source was located for it, and the three subdivisions are not independent of one another. This clause states the statute's own findings and its continuing-duty language; it does not itself describe the mechanics of the preliminary or final declaration of disclosure, which are addressed in other clauses of this document.

TWO SEPARATE, SEQUENTIAL DISCLOSURES ARE REQUIRED: PRELIMINARY AND FINAL
California law requires each party to a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation to serve on the other party two separate statutory disclosures: a preliminary declaration of disclosure, and — unless waived or not required under a statutory exception — a final declaration of disclosure. Each party must also file proof of service of each declaration with the court. The preliminary declaration and the final declaration are governed by distinct statutory sections, each with its own content requirements, timing, and (for the final declaration only) a mutual-waiver mechanism, addressed in other clauses of this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In order to provide full and accurate disclosure of all assets and liabilities in which one or both parties may have an interest, each party to a proceeding for dissolution of the marriage or legal separation of the parties shall serve on the other party a preliminary declaration of disclosure under Section 2104, unless service of the preliminary declaration of disclosure is waived as provided in Section 2107 or is not required pursuant to Section 2110, and a final declaration of disclosure under Section 2105, unless service of the final declaration of disclosure is waived pursuant to Section 2105, 2107, or 2110, and shall file proof of service of each with the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2103 (California Legislative Information text), the requirement to serve both a preliminary and a final declaration of disclosure, and to file proof of service of each (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2103.)

This is a single statutory section (section 2103); no additional independent source was located for it. This clause references, but does not independently describe, the statutory exceptions this section itself cross-references for waiving service of the preliminary declaration (section 2107, addressed in a separate clause of this document) and for when service is not required at all (section 2110, governing default judgments) — section 2110's default-judgment-specific procedure was not independently re-verified for this document and is not described here.

THE PRELIMINARY DECLARATION OF DISCLOSURE: REQUIRED CONTENT AND SERVICE DEADLINES
The preliminary declaration of disclosure must be executed under penalty of perjury on a form prescribed by the Judicial Council, and must include all tax returns filed by the declarant within the two years preceding the date the party served the declaration. The statute states that the commission of perjury on the preliminary declaration of disclosure may be grounds for setting aside the judgment, in addition to any other civil or criminal remedies otherwise available for perjury. The preliminary declaration must set forth, with enough particularity that a person of reasonable and ordinary intelligence can ascertain it: the identity of all assets in which the declarant has or may have an interest and all liabilities for which the declarant is or may be liable, regardless of whether the asset or liability is characterized as community, quasi-community, or separate property; and, where property is not solely owned by one or both parties, the declarant's percentage of ownership in each asset and percentage of obligation for each liability (the declarant may also, but is not required to, state a characterization of each asset or liability). On timing: the petitioner must serve the preliminary declaration of disclosure either concurrently with the petition for dissolution or legal separation, or within 60 days of filing the petition (or, where the summons and petition were served by publication or posting and the respondent files a response before a default judgment is entered, within 30 days of that response being filed); the respondent must serve it either concurrently with the response to the petition, or within 60 days of filing the response. These time periods may be extended by the parties' written agreement or by court order.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except by court order for good cause, as provided in Section 2107, or when service of the preliminary declaration of disclosure is not required pursuant to Section 2110, in the time period set forth in subdivision (f), each party shall serve on the other party a preliminary declaration of disclosure, executed under penalty of perjury on a form prescribed by the Judicial Council. The commission of perjury on the preliminary declaration of disclosure may be grounds for setting aside the judgment, or any part or parts thereof, pursuant to Chapter 10 (commencing with Section 2120), in addition to any and all other remedies, civil or criminal, that otherwise are available under law for the commission of perjury. The preliminary declaration of disclosure shall include all tax returns filed by the declarant within the two years prior to the date that the party served the declaration."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2104(a) (California Legislative Information text), the perjury execution requirement, the two-year tax return content requirement, and the perjury-based ground for setting aside a judgment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2104.)
  "The preliminary declaration of disclosure shall set forth with sufficient particularity, that a person of reasonable and ordinary intelligence can ascertain, all of the following: (1) The identity of all assets in which the declarant has or may have an interest and all liabilities for which the declarant is or may be liable, regardless of the characterization of the asset or liability as community, quasi-community, or separate. (2) The declarant’s percentage of ownership in each asset and percentage of obligation for each liability when property is not solely owned by one or both of the parties. The preliminary declaration may also set forth the declarant’s characterization of each asset or liability."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2104(c) (California Legislative Information text), the particularity standard for identifying assets, liabilities, and ownership/obligation percentages (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2104.)
  "The petitioner shall serve the other party with the preliminary declaration of disclosure either concurrently with the petition for dissolution or legal separation, or within 60 days of filing the petition. When a petitioner serves the summons and petition by publication or posting pursuant to court order and the respondent files a response prior to a default judgment being entered, the petitioner shall serve the other party with the preliminary declaration of disclosure within 30 days of the response being filed. The respondent shall serve the other party with the preliminary declaration of disclosure either concurrently with the response to the petition, or within 60 days of filing the response. The time periods specified in this subdivision may be extended by written agreement of the parties or by court order."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2104(f) (California Legislative Information text), the service deadlines for the petitioner and respondent, and the extension mechanism (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2104.)

This clause quotes three subdivisions of a single statutory section (section 2104(a), (c), and (f)); they are not independent of one another, though each states a distinct rule (the perjury/tax-return content requirement, the particularity-of-content standard, and the service deadlines). This clause does not describe section 2104(b) (the rule against filing the preliminary declaration with the court absent a court order) or section 2104(d)-(e) (the right to amend without leave of court, and the accompanying income and expense declaration requirement) — those subdivisions were fetched as part of the same primary-source text but are not restated or quoted here.

THE FINAL DECLARATION OF DISCLOSURE: REQUIRED CONTENT, TIMING, AND THE MUTUAL WAIVER
Unless the parties mutually waive it, each party (or that party's attorney) must serve on the other party a final declaration of disclosure and a current income and expense declaration, executed under penalty of perjury on a form prescribed by the Judicial Council. The statute ties the service deadline to whichever of two events occurs: absent a court order for good cause, service must occur before or at the time the parties enter into an agreement resolving property or support issues other than pendente lite support, or, if the case goes to trial, no later than 45 days before the first assigned trial date. As with the preliminary declaration, the statute states that the commission of perjury on the final declaration of disclosure may be grounds for setting aside the judgment, in addition to any other civil or criminal remedies otherwise available for perjury. The final declaration must include all material facts and information regarding: the characterization of all assets and liabilities; the valuation of all assets contended to be community property or in which the community is contended to have an interest; the amounts of all obligations contended to be community obligations or for which the community is contended to have liability; and the earnings, accumulations, and expenses of each party as set forth in the income and expense declaration. California law does allow the parties to waive the final declaration of disclosure, but only by mutual stipulation, executed under penalty of perjury, entered in open court or by separate stipulation — and only where that waiver includes specific representations: that both parties have complied with the preliminary-declaration statute and have completed and exchanged their preliminary declarations; that both parties have completed and exchanged a current income and expense declaration covering all material facts about that party's earnings, accumulations, and expenses; that both parties have fully complied with the parties' ongoing disclosure obligations under Family Code section 2102 and have fully augmented their preliminary declarations with all material facts on characterization, valuation, and the amount of obligations; that the waiver is knowing, intelligent, and voluntary; and that each party understands the waiver does not limit the parties' underlying legal disclosure obligations — it is only a sworn statement that those obligations have already been fulfilled — and that noncompliance with those obligations will still result in the court setting aside the judgment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except by court order for good cause, before or at the time the parties enter into an agreement for the resolution of property or support issues other than pendente lite support, or, if the case goes to trial, no later than 45 days before the first assigned trial date, each party, or the attorney for the party in this matter, shall serve on the other party a final declaration of disclosure and a current income and expense declaration, executed under penalty of perjury on a form prescribed by the Judicial Council, unless the parties mutually waive the final declaration of disclosure. The commission of perjury on the final declaration of disclosure by a party may be grounds for setting aside the judgment, or any part or parts thereof, pursuant to Chapter 10 (commencing with Section 2120), in addition to any and all other remedies, civil or criminal, that otherwise are available under law for the commission of perjury."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2105(a) (California Legislative Information text), the service obligation, the two triggering deadlines, and the perjury-based ground for setting aside a judgment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2105.)
  "The final declaration of disclosure shall include all of the following information: (1) All material facts and information regarding the characterization of all assets and liabilities. (2) All material facts and information regarding the valuation of all assets that are contended to be community property or in which it is contended the community has an interest. (3) All material facts and information regarding the amounts of all obligations that are contended to be community obligations or for which it is contended the community has liability. (4) All material facts and information regarding the earnings, accumulations, and expenses of each party that have been set forth in the income and expense declaration."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2105(b) (California Legislative Information text), the required content of the final declaration of disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2105.)
  "The parties may stipulate to a mutual waiver of the requirements of subdivision (a) concerning the final declaration of disclosure, by execution of a waiver under penalty of perjury entered into in open court or by separate stipulation. The waiver shall include all of the following representations: (1) Both parties have complied with Section 2104 and the preliminary declarations of disclosure have been completed and exchanged. (2) Both parties have completed and exchanged a current income and expense declaration, that includes all material facts and information regarding that party’s earnings, accumulations, and expenses. (3) Both parties have fully complied with Section 2102 and have fully augmented the preliminary declarations of disclosure, including disclosure of all material facts and information regarding the characterization of all assets and liabilities, the valuation of all assets that are contended to be community property or in which it is contended the community has an interest, and the amounts of all obligations that are contended to be community obligations or for which it is contended the community has liability. (4) The waiver is knowingly, intelligently, and voluntarily entered into by each of the parties. (5) Each party understands that this waiver does not limit the legal disclosure obligations of the parties, but rather is a statement under penalty of perjury that those obligations have been fulfilled. Each party further understands that noncompliance with those obligations will result in the court setting aside the judgment."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2105(d) (California Legislative Information text), the mutual-waiver mechanism and its five required representations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2105.)

This clause does not restate section 2105(c) (the court's authority, in setting aside a judgment for noncompliance with this section, to limit the set-aside to the portions of the judgment materially affected by the nondisclosure) — that subdivision was fetched as part of the same primary-source text but is addressed only in this document's separate noncompliance-consequences clause. CONSEQUENCES OF NONCOMPLIANCE: MANDATORY MONETARY SANCTIONS AND SETTING ASIDE THE JUDGMENT
California's disclosure statute states specific consequences for a party's noncompliance, separate from the perjury-based grounds for setting aside a judgment described elsewhere in this document. First, sanctions: if a party fails to comply with any provision of the disclosure chapter, the statute states that the court shall, in addition to any other remedy provided by law, impose money sanctions against the noncomplying party, in an amount sufficient to deter repetition of the conduct, and that the sanction shall include reasonable attorney's fees, costs incurred, or both, unless the court finds the noncomplying party acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the sanction unjust. Second, setting aside the judgment: except as otherwise provided, if a court enters a judgment when the parties have failed to comply with all of the chapter's disclosure requirements, the statute states that the court shall set aside the judgment, and that the failure to comply does not constitute harmless error. A narrower rule applies where the complying party has already obtained a court-granted voluntary waiver of receiving the noncomplying party's preliminary declaration: in that circumstance, the court sets aside the judgment only at the complying party's request, unless the motion to set aside is instead based on actual fraud that kept the defrauded party ignorant of, or fraudulently prevented from fully participating in, the proceeding, or on perjury (as defined in Penal Code section 118) in the preliminary or final declaration, in the waiver of the final declaration, or in the current income and expense statement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If a party fails to comply with any provision of this chapter, the court shall, in addition to any other remedy provided by law, impose money sanctions against the noncomplying party. Sanctions shall be in an amount sufficient to deter repetition of the conduct or comparable conduct, and shall include reasonable attorney’s fees, costs incurred, or both, unless the court finds that the noncomplying party acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2107(c) (California Legislative Information text), the mandatory money-sanctions remedy for noncompliance with any provision of the disclosure chapter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2107.)
  "Except as otherwise provided in this subdivision, if a court enters a judgment when the parties have failed to comply with all disclosure requirements of this chapter, the court shall set aside the judgment. The failure to comply with the disclosure requirements does not constitute harmless error. If the court granted the complying party’s voluntary waiver of receipt of the noncomplying party’s preliminary declaration of disclosure pursuant to paragraph (3) of subdivision (b), the court shall set aside the judgment only at the request of the complying party, unless the motion to set aside the judgment is based on one of the following: (1) Actual fraud if the defrauded party was kept in ignorance or in some other manner was fraudulently prevented from fully participating in the proceeding. (2) Perjury, as defined in Section 118 of the Penal Code, in the preliminary or final declaration of disclosure, in the waiver of the final declaration of disclosure, or in the current income and expense statement."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2107(d) (California Legislative Information text), the mandatory set-aside-the-judgment consequence for a failure to comply with the disclosure requirements, and its exceptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2107.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific California consequences for noncompliance with the disclosure requirements — not a claim about whether any specific party's disclosure was or was not compliant, or about what remedy a court would actually order in any specific case. This clause quotes two subdivisions of a single statutory section (section 2107(c) and (d)); they are not independent of one another. This clause does not describe section 2107(a)-(b) (the complying party's procedural options — requesting further particularity, then moving to compel a further response, to preclude evidence, or to obtain a voluntary waiver of the noncomplying party's declaration — that precede the sanctions and set-aside consequences in subdivisions (c)-(d)) or section 2107(e) (the court's authority, on a motion to set aside, to order production of the exchanged declarations, which are otherwise returned to the parties rather than filed with the court) — those subdivisions were fetched as part of the same primary-source text but are not restated or quoted here.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

The respondent shall serve the other party with the preliminary declaration of disclosure either concurrently with the response to the petition, or within 60 days of filing the response. The time periods specified in this subdivision may be extended by written agreement of the parties or by court order.

expectedJSON.body: Unless the parties mutually waive it, each party (or that party's attorney) must serve on the other party a final declaration of disclosure and a current income and expense declaration, executed under penalty of perjury on a form prescribed by the Judicial Council. The statute ties the service deadline to whichever of two events occurs: absent a court order for good cause, service must occur before or at the time the parties enter into an agreement resolving property or support issues other than pendente lite support, or, if the case goes to trial, no later than 45 days before the first assigned trial date. As with the preliminary declaration, the statute states that the commission of perjury on the final declaration of disclosure may be grounds for setting aside the judgment, in addition to any other civil or criminal remedies otherwise available for perjury. The final declaration must include all material facts and information regarding: the characterization of all assets and liabilities; the valuation of all assets contended to be community property or in which the community is contended to have an interest; the amounts of all obligations contended to be community obligations or for which the community is contended to have liability; and the earnings, accumulations, and expenses of each party as set forth in the income and expense declaration. California law does allow the parties to waive the final declaration of disclosure, but only by mutual stipulation, executed under penalty of perjury, entered in open court or by separate stipulation — and only where that waiver includes specific representations: that both parties have complied with the preliminary-declaration statute and have completed and exchanged their preliminary declarations; that both parties have completed and exchanged a current income and expense declaration covering all material facts about that party's earnings, accumulations, and expenses; that both parties have fully complied with the parties' ongoing disclosure obligations under Family Code section 2102 and have fully augmented their preliminary declarations with all material facts on characterization, valuation, and the amount of obligations; that the waiver is knowing, intelligent, and voluntary; and that each party understands the waiver does not limit the parties' underlying legal disclosure obligations — it is only a sworn statement that those obligations have already been fulfilled — and that noncompliance with those obligations will still result in the court setting aside the judgment.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2105(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the service obligation, the two triggering deadlines, and the perjury-based ground for setting aside a judgment
citations.quote: Except by court order for good cause, before or at the time the parties enter into an agreement for the resolution of property or support issues other than pendente lite support, or, if the case goes to trial, no later than 45 days before the first assigned trial date, each party, or the attorney for the party in this matter, shall serve on the other party a final declaration of disclosure and a current income and expense declaration, executed under penalty of perjury on a form prescribed by the Judicial Council, unless the parties mutually waive the final declaration of disclosure. The commission of perjury on the final declaration of disclosure by a party may be grounds for setting aside the judgment, or any part or parts thereof, pursuant to Chapter 10 (commencing with Section 2120), in addition to any and all other remedies, civil or criminal, that otherwise are available under law for the commission of perjury.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2105(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the required content of the final declaration of disclosure
citations.quote: The final declaration of disclosure shall include all of the following information: (1) All material facts and information regarding the characterization of all assets and liabilities. (2) All material facts and information regarding the valuation of all assets that are contended to be community property or in which it is contended the community has an interest. (3) All material facts and information regarding the amounts of all obligations that are contended to be community obligations or for which it is contended the community has liability. (4) All material facts and information regarding the earnings, accumulations, and expenses of each party that have been set forth in the income and expense declaration.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2105(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mutual-waiver mechanism and its five required representations
citations.quote: The parties may stipulate to a mutual waiver of the requirements of subdivision (a) concerning the final declaration of disclosure, by execution of a waiver under penalty of perjury entered into in open court or by separate stipulation. The waiver shall include all of the following representations: (1) Both parties have complied with Section 2104 and the preliminary declarations of disclosure have been completed and exchanged. (2) Both parties have completed and exchanged a current income and expense declaration, that includes all material facts and information regarding that party’s earnings, accumulations, and expenses. (3) Both parties have fully complied with Section 2102 and have fully augmented the preliminary declarations of disclosure, including disclosure of all material facts and information regarding the characterization of all assets and liabilities, the valuation of all assets that are contended to be community property or in which it is contended the community has an interest, and the amounts of all obligations that are contended to be community obligations or for which it is contended the community has liability. (4) The waiver is knowingly, intelligently, and voluntarily entered into by each of the parties. (5) Each party understands that this waiver does not limit the legal disclosure obligations of the parties, but rather is a statement under penalty of perjury that those obligations have been fulfilled. Each party further understands that noncompliance with those obligations will result in the court setting aside the judgment.

expectedJSON.body: California's disclosure statute states specific consequences for a party's noncompliance, separate from the perjury-based grounds for setting aside a judgment described elsewhere in this document. First, sanctions: if a party fails to comply with any provision of the disclosure chapter, the statute states that the court shall, in addition to any other remedy provided by law, impose money sanctions against the noncomplying party, in an amount sufficient to deter repetition of the conduct, and that the sanction shall include reasonable attorney's fees, costs incurred, or both, unless the court finds the noncomplying party acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the sanction unjust. Second, setting aside the judgment: except as otherwise provided, if a court enters a judgment when the parties have failed to comply with all of the chapter's disclosure requirements, the statute states that the court shall set aside the judgment, and that the failure to comply does not constitute harmless error. A narrower rule applies where the complying party has already obtained a court-granted voluntary waiver of receiving the noncomplying party's preliminary declaration: in that circumstance, the court sets aside the judgment only at the complying party's request, unless the motion to set aside is instead based on actual fraud that kept the defrauded party ignorant of, or fraudulently prevented from fully participating in, the proceeding, or on perjury (as defined in Penal Code section 118) in the preliminary or final declaration, in the waiver of the final declaration, or in the current income and expense statement.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2107(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mandatory money-sanctions remedy for noncompliance with any provision of the disclosure chapter
citations.quote: If a party fails to comply with any provision of this chapter, the court shall, in addition to any other remedy provided by law, impose money sanctions against the noncomplying party. Sanctions shall be in an amount sufficient to deter repetition of the conduct or comparable conduct, and shall include reasonable attorney’s fees, costs incurred, or both, unless the court finds that the noncomplying party acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2107(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mandatory set-aside-the-judgment consequence for a failure to comply with the disclosure requirements, and its exceptions
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this subdivision, if a court enters a judgment when the parties have failed to comply with all disclosure requirements of this chapter, the court shall set aside the judgment. The failure to comply with the disclosure requirements does not constitute harmless error. If the court granted the complying party’s voluntary waiver of receipt of the noncomplying party’s preliminary declaration of disclosure pursuant to paragraph (3) of subdivision (b), the court shall set aside the judgment only at the request of the complying party, unless the motion to set aside the judgment is based on one of the following: (1) Actual fraud if the defrauded party was kept in ignorance or in some other manner was fraudulently prevented from fully participating in the proceeding. (2) Perjury, as defined in Section 118 of the Penal Code, in the preliminary or final declaration of disclosure, in the waiver of the final declaration of disclosure, or in the current income and expense statement.
